title: What Is the Average Salary in Melbourne? Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay
description: Find out how to convert your hourly rate to annual salary using 38-hour weeks. Learn about the average salary in Melbourne, tax, super, and minimum wage in Australia.
salarySummary: For a 38-hour week, your annual gross pay is your hourly rate multiplied by 38 hours per week and 52 weeks per year.

faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week (usually 38 for full-time) and then by 52 weeks. For example, $30 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $59,280 per year. Your fortnightly pay is your weekly pay multiplied by two.

faqs.q: What is the average salary in Melbourne?
faqs.a: The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports national average full-time adult ordinary time earnings of $2,083.70 per week (May 2026). The average salary in Melbourne may differ from the national figure. For a precise average salary in Melbourne, refer to ABS state-level earnings data for Victoria.

faqs.q: Does the annual figure include superannuation?
faqs.a: No. Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at 12% (subject to the $270,830 maximum contribution base). The annual figure shown here is gross pay before tax and before super is added.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Annual Salary from Your Hourly Rate

When you have an hourly rate or a salary offer, the first step is to convert it to an annual figure. The standard formula is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**

For full-time employees, we assume a 38-hour week, which is the ordinary hours used by the Fair Work Ombudsman and the Australian Bureau of Statistics. For example, if your hourly rate is $30, your annual pay would be $30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. Your fortnightly pay would be $30 × 38 × 2 = $2,280.

This calculation assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. It is a starting point for comparing offers or understanding your potential earnings.

## The National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The National Minimum Wage, set by the Fair Work Commission, is $26.44 per hour from 1 July 2026. For a 38-hour week, that equals $1,004.90 per week. Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base rate, making the casual minimum $33.05 per hour. **Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading** into the timesheet; instead, use the checkbox to add the 25% loading on top of your base rate.

Many employees are covered by award rates, which are often higher than the National Minimum Wage. Awards set minimum pay for specific industries and occupations. Your award rate may include allowances, penalty rates for weekends or nights, and overtime. The annual conversion here does not account for those extras, so your actual annual earnings could be higher if you regularly work unsocial hours.

Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. That means if your annual gross is $59,280, your employer would contribute an additional $7,113.60 to your super fund.

## Average Earnings and the Average Salary in Melbourne

The Australian Bureau of Statistics publishes Average Weekly Earnings (AWE) data. For May 2026, full-time adult ordinary time earnings averaged $2,083.70 per week nationally. That equates to an annual salary of approximately $108,352.40. When all employees (including part-time and casual) are included, total average weekly earnings are $1,579.20, or about $82,118.40 per year.

These are national averages. The average salary in Melbourne may differ because wages vary by state and territory. For instance, Victoria’s average weekly earnings can be higher or lower than the national figure depending on industry mix and economic conditions. To find the average salary in Melbourne, you would need to consult ABS state-level data for Victoria. While we cannot provide a precise figure here, the national averages give you a benchmark.

If you are comparing a job offer in Melbourne, remember that the average salary in Melbourne is just one data point. Your own pay will depend on your occupation, experience, and the specific employer. The [reference tables](/data) on this site can help you explore broader pay ranges.

## Tax and Superannuation Considerations

Once you have your annual gross pay, you need to consider tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 income year, the resident tax rates are:

- Nil on income up to $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

The Medicare levy is generally 2% of your taxable income. Low-income earners may qualify for a reduction, but the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here, so we use the 2025–26 single thresholds for estimates. The [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page provides more detail on net pay calculations.

Superannuation is not deducted from your gross pay; it is paid on top by your employer. The 12% super guarantee applies to ordinary time earnings up to $270,830 per year. If your annual gross exceeds that cap, super is only paid on the first $270,830. Salary packaging, the Medicare levy surcharge, and HELP repayments are not included in these estimates.

## Using Our Tools

To calculate your own annual pay, use [the timesheet](/) on this site. Enter your base hourly rate, and if you are a casual employee, tick the casual loading checkbox to add 25% on top. The timesheet will show your weekly, fortnightly, and annual gross pay, along with an estimate of tax and super.

For more detailed information on award rates and industry pay, visit the [pay guides](/blog) section. You can also explore [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) and [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) topics.

Remember that the figures here are estimates. Your actual pay may differ due to overtime, allowances, penalty rates, or salary sacrifice. Always check your employment contract and consult the Fair Work Ombudsman for your specific award or agreement.
